title: The Sharpe Pint: Tariffs, Tightening, and the CFO Survival Rate

opening_mood.text: Welcome back to the desk. If you spent the long weekend successfully pretending that spreadsheets don't exist, we have some rather spicy news: the autumn term has kicked off with absolute chaos. We have got retaliatory tariffs landing on the Canadian border, Brent crude knocking on the door of $100, and central banks dusting off their hawkish feathers. Grab a strong coffee; here is your morning briefing.

content.text: Canada Hits Back: Carney's $20 Billion Tariff Wall Goes Live

Just after midnight, Canada's retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of US goods officially took effect. This follows the dramatic collapse of trade negotiations last month, when Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended talks, calling US terms 'unfair' and 'uneconomic'. Not to be outdone, US President Donald Trump fired back, warning that Canadian business jet maker Bombardier will be blocked from selling its planes in the US unless it moves manufacturing south of the border.

items: Why it matters: This is a major escalation with the US's largest trading partner. It injects a fresh dose of supply-chain friction and inflationary pressure right into the North American economy.

The City angle: For equity analysts, this is a headache for industrials, transport, and consumer-sensitive stocks. For macro desks, it is another supply-side shock that complicates the inflation outlook.

What to say at work: 'Carney isn't playing ball. With $20 billion of tariffs hitting today and Trump targeting Bombardier, we are looking at a real supply-chain headache. It is going to feed straight back into the inflation narrative just as the Fed is trying to figure out its next move.'

content.text: The Death of the Easy Autumn: UBS's Dramatic Fed U-Turn

Following Friday's surprisingly robust August jobs report—where US non-farm payrolls jumped by 162,000 (smashing the consensus of 53,000)—UBS Global Wealth Management has executed a dramatic U-turn. The Swiss bank now expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates twice before the end of 2026 (in September and December), completely reversing its previous forecast of no policy changes this year. Markets are now pricing in a 58% to 60% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the upcoming September 15–16 meeting.

items: Why it matters: The 'rate cut' or 'long pause' consensus is officially dead. The 10-year US Treasury yield is hovering near 4.80% as bond markets adjust to a 'higher-for-longer' reality.

The City angle: Fixed income desks are scrambling to reprice risk. If you are interviewing for macro or credit roles, expect to be grilled on how a September hike will impact corporate debt refinancing.

What to say at work: 'UBS doing a complete 180 on their Fed call is the perfect example of how quickly the macro narrative can flip. A 162k payroll print has turned what was supposed to be a quiet autumn into a scramble. If this week's CPI print comes in hot, that September hike is a lock.'

content.text: Oil Flirts with $100 as Strait of Hormuz Clashes Flare

Brent crude spiked to $99.73 a barrel, while WTI gained to $94.28, reaching multi-week highs. The rally was triggered by an escalating military conflict between the US and Iran in the crucial Strait of Hormuz. Iran issued fresh warnings that it will 'take action against any threat, even before it is carried out,' raising fears of prolonged disruptions to global oil supplies.

items: Why it matters: Energy is the ultimate inflation wildcard. A sustained run toward $100 oil will squeeze corporate margins and consumer wallets, making the Fed's job almost impossible.

The City angle: Energy traders are printing money, but equity markets are rotating. Tech is showing relative strength as a defensive growth play, while the Dow and small-caps are bearing the brunt of rising energy and rate pressures.

What to say at work: 'Brent kissing $100 is the real wildcard here. The Strait of Hormuz skirmishes are putting a massive geopolitical risk premium back into energy. It makes the Fed's job almost impossible—how do you manage supply-side energy shocks with demand-side rate hikes?'

content.text: From Hatchbacks to the Iron Dome: VW Repurposes Osnabrück Factory

In a fascinating sign of the times, Volkswagen has agreed to sell its Osnabrück plant to Tel Aviv-based private equity firm Aurelius Capital and the German state of Lower Saxony. The new owners plan to convert the struggling car factory into a defence production hub, partnering with Israel's Rafael Advanced Defense Systems to manufacture components for the Iron Dome air defence system. The deal cleverly bypasses opposition from Qatar's sovereign wealth fund (which holds a 10% voting stake in VW and tried to block the Rafael partnership).

items: Why it matters: It is the ultimate symbol of Europe's shifting industrial base. As the European automotive sector struggles with Chinese EV competition, idle capacity is being redirected into a booming, state-funded defence sector.
The City angle: This is a masterclass in PE-led restructuring and geopolitical manoeuvring. It preserves 1,200 jobs while tapping into Berlin's massive defence-spending expansion.

What to say at work: 'VW selling its Osnabrück plant to turn it into an Iron Dome component factory is the ultimate sign of the times. It is a neat PE-led workaround to bypass Qatar's veto, and it shows how Europe's industrial base is shifting from cars to defence tech.'

content.text: The $3.9 Billion Regional Bank Reverse Merger: WaFd and EverBank's PE-Backed Marriage

WaFd, Inc. (Washington Federal) has entered a $3.9 billion reverse merger with EverBank Financial Corp. Upon completion, EverBank's heavy-hitting private equity backers—including Stone Point Capital, Warburg Pincus, Reverence Capital Partners, Sixth Street, and Bayview Asset Management, alongside TIAA—will collectively own 59.2% of the combined public company, with WaFd shareholders owning 40.8%.

items: Why it matters: This is a highly creative exit and scale play. Instead of a traditional IPO, EverBank's PE sponsors are backing into a public listing to rapidly scale up fee-income streams and Registered Investment Advisor (RIA) offerings.

The City angle: M&A desks will view this as a blueprint for regional bank consolidation. It proves that private equity is still highly active in financial services, using structured mergers to achieve public scale.

What to say at work: 'The WaFd-EverBank reverse merger is a classic PE play. Stone Point, Warburg, and Sixth Street are essentially backing into a public listing to scale up fee income and RIA offerings. It shows the regional banking consolidation trend is far from over, and PE is driving the bus.'

content.text: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1: The Rise of the Persistent Agent

Anthropic has launched Claude Fable 5.1 (alongside a restricted version, Mythos 5.1, for cyber and bio research). Fable 5.1 is a massive agentic upgrade designed for long-running, multi-hour tasks like codebase-wide refactoring and complex financial modelling. Crucially, Anthropic slashed cache read pricing by 75%, bringing down typical API costs by 25% to 45%. They also introduced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) in partnership with AWS, allowing enterprise clients to use the model with zero data retention (ZDR) in their own controlled cloud environments.

items: Why it matters: The AI race is shifting from 'who has the smartest chatbot' to 'who can run autonomous agents cheaply and securely'. The 75% cut in cache pricing makes agentic workflows commercially viable at scale.

The City angle: This is a massive deal for quant funds and investment banks. Compliance departments that previously blocked LLMs over data privacy concerns now have a clear path to deployment via AWS's zero data retention safeguards.

What to say at work: 'Fable 5.1 isn't just about being smarter; it's about being persistent and cheaper. The 75% cut in cache read pricing makes agentic workflows actually viable at scale. Plus, the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards are exactly what compliance departments need to finally let us use these models on proprietary data.'

content.text: The Post-Labour Day Hangover: Oil, Tariffs, and the Return of the Hawks

Welcome back from the long weekend. If you were hoping for a gentle slide into autumn, the markets have other ideas. With US traders returning from the Labour Day holiday, they are staring down a cocktail of surging crude, an escalating trade war across the Canadian border, and a bond market that is suddenly looking very twitchy about central bank hikes.
Crude Nears $100 as the Strait of Hormuz Flares Up

The biggest mover of the morning is Brent crude, which is aggressively knocking on the door of $100 a barrel, trading up at $99.24. This isn't just a minor supply hiccup; it is a full-blown geopolitical risk premium. A fresh wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Aramco infrastructure, combined with escalating US-Iran clashes in the Strait of Hormuz, has traders scrambling. Tehran is reportedly finalising an agreement with Oman to establish a new shipping corridor, aiming for complete control over the strait. For equity markets, this is a double whammy. Higher oil is an immediate tax on global growth, and it throws a massive spanner in the works for the 'inflation is dead' narrative. S&P 500 futures are down 0.3%, Dow futures are off 0.7%, and the pan-European Stoxx 600 has slipped 0.2% to 648.41.
The Great Canadian Standoff: Carney vs. Trump

If Middle Eastern geopolitics weren't enough, we now have a trade war on our doorstep. Just after midnight, Canada's retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion of US goods took effect. Prime Minister Mark Carney is playing hardball after trade negotiations collapsed, responding to Donald Trump's 50% levies on Canadian exports. Trump has already retaliated on social media, threatening to ban Bombardier business jets from the US unless they are built domestically. For multi-asset desks, this is a reminder that supply-chain friction is back on the menu, and it is inherently inflationary.
Rates: The Return of the Hawk

Underneath the hood, the real action is in the rates market. Remember Friday's US jobs report? Nonfarm payrolls blew past expectations, printing at 162,000 for August against a consensus of just 50,000. That hot print has completely flipped the script for the Federal Reserve's September 15-16 meeting. Traders are now pricing in a 63% probability of a rate hike. The US 10-year Treasury yield has crept up to 4.81%. Meanwhile, on this side of the pond, the European Central Bank is widely expected to deliver a 25-basis-point hike this Thursday. Deutsche Bank is already calling for another quarter-point move in December. If you thought central banks were done squeezing, think again.
FX: The Yen's Revenge

The FX market is where the cross-asset read gets really interesting. The Japanese Yen is on an absolute tear, surging to its strongest level since February. USD/JPY has smashed through the critical 155 support level and is trading down near 153.50. Why? It is a classic policy divergence trade. While the Fed is debating a hike, the Bank of Japan is actually preparing to move. Kyodo reported that the BOJ plans to raise rates by 25 basis points to 1.25% at its September 18 meeting. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also been talking up a stronger yen, and Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama basically gave the market a green light overnight by saying Tokyo is perfectly comfortable with the yen's appreciation. The casualty here is Japanese equities. The Nikkei 225 tumbled 1.7% to 65,269.33 as exporters got hammered—Toyota shed 4.1% and Panasonic dropped 5.8%.
Single Stock Stories: Novartis and Computacenter

items: Novartis (-8.8%): The Swiss pharma giant is having a shocker. After its experimental cholesterol drug pelacarsen failed a late-stage trial on Monday, its myotonic dystrophy drug del-desiran missed its primary endpoint on Tuesday. That is back-to-back Phase III failures, wiping billions off its market cap.

Computacenter (+3.8%): On the brighter side, the London-listed IT firm jumped after raising its full-year profit guidance to 'no less than £380 million' (well ahead of the £341 million consensus), proving that data-centre and digital infrastructure spending is still a goldmine.
Dunelm (-10%): The homewares retailer slumped after reporting flat annual profits and announcing a three-year plan to slash £100 million in 'unproductive costs' to save and reinvest.

content.text: The Pub Talk Takeaway

If you're chatting with colleagues or clients today, the key talking point is the shift from 'growth worries' to 'inflation and rate worries.' The combination of $99 oil, a US-Canada trade war, and a hot US jobs report means the 'higher-for-longer' rate narrative is getting a second wind. The Yen's massive rally is also unwinding the last of the global carry trades, which explains why risk assets are feeling heavy. Keep an eye on US CPI later this week—if that comes in hot, expect the bond market to have a proper tantrum.

content.text: The Magic of 'Four-Wall EBITDA' (And Why You Can't Drink It)

Imagine you are looking to buy a trendy chain of London craft beer pubs. The broker hands you the pitch deck, and the headline numbers look a bit depressing: a 12% EBITDA margin. In the City, that is the financial equivalent of a lukewarm, flat pint. But before you bin the deck, you look closer and spot a metric called 'Four-Wall EBITDA' (sometimes called store-level or restaurant-level EBITDA) sitting at a beautiful 30%. What is going on here?

Four-Wall EBITDA is the profitability of a single physical location (a pub, a gym, a retail store, or even a dental clinic) before any central corporate overhead (G&A) is allocated to it. It isolates the pure unit economics of the concept. It asks: 'If we ignore the expensive Soho HQ, the CEO's salary, and the central HR team, does this specific shop actually make money?'
The Math: A Tale of Ten Pubs
Let us look at a simple example. Suppose our pub chain has 10 sites:

items: Total Revenue: £10,000,000 (£1,000,000 average per pub).
Site-Level Costs: Each pub spends £700,000 on beer, bar staff, rent, utilities, and local business rates.
Four-Wall EBITDA: Each pub generates £300,000. Across all 10 sites, that is £3,000,000 of Four-Wall EBITDA (a 30% Four-Wall Margin).
Corporate HQ Costs: The company spends £1,800,000 on central overheads (the CEO, a finance team, central marketing, and HR).
Consolidated EBITDA: £3,000,000 minus £1,800,000 leaves you with £1,200,000 (a 12% consolidated margin).

content.text: To a lazy investor, this looks like a mediocre business. But to a Private Equity (PE) sponsor or a strategic consolidator, it is an absolute goldmine. Why? Because of the way physical businesses scale.
Why the City Cares: The Platform Play
In asset management and private equity, Four-Wall EBITDA is the holy grail for two reasons:

items: The Synergy Arbitrage: If a PE firm already owns a larger pub platform, they do not need the target's £1.8m HQ. They can fire the target's CEO, merge the finance teams, and run the 10 pubs using their existing corporate infrastructure. Most of that £1.8m G&A vanishes, instantly boosting the consolidated EBITDA from £1.2m to nearly £3m.

The Growth Runway: It proves whether the concept is actually replicable. If you open an 11th pub, it will not require a new CEO or a new HR director. It will just cost the site-level capex and, if the unit economics hold, it will drop another £300,000 of high-margin cash flow straight to the bottom line.

content.text: The Classic Trap: The Phantom Margin

The biggest beginner mistake is valuing a business solely on a multiple of Four-Wall EBITDA and forgetting that corporate overhead is a real, non-discretionary cash expense. You cannot run a 50-store empire from a laptop at a kitchen table. If a broker tries to sell you a business on '10x Four-Wall EBITDA' without factoring in the necessary G&A required to support those stores, you are going to massively overpay. Always ask: 'What is the fully loaded, post-G&A EBITDA?'
How to Use This in an Interview

If you are interviewing for a role in Private Equity, Investment Banking, or Equity Research and get a case study on a multi-unit consumer business (retailers, restaurants, gyms, car washes), do not just ask for 'EBITDA'. Ask: 'What are the four-wall margins versus the consolidated margins, and how much of the G&A is truly fixed versus variable platform cost?' This immediately signals that you understand the operational reality of scaling a physical footprint.
Over a Pint: Sound Smart at the Pub

"The consolidated numbers look a bit soft, but if you strip out the corporate empire-building, the four-wall EBITDA is over 30%. They have basically built a FTSE 250-sized HQ to run just 10 sites. If we acquire them and plug them into our existing platform, we can cut the G&A in half and capture incredible unit-level economics."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Matched Filter: Why Your Deep Learning Model is Choking on Order Flow

We've all been there. You've got a rich dataset of institutional order flow, and you want to predict stock returns. Naturally, you throw the kitchen sink at it: an LSTM, some attention layers, maybe a bit of wavelet denoising. But the model keeps spitting out garbage, collapsing to the unconditional mean. So you assume the signal is dead.

But as a pair of brilliant papers by researcher Sungwoo Kang points out, the problem isn't the signal—it's how you're normalising it. Specifically, the standard practice of dividing net order flow by daily trading volume (to get a 'participation rate') is actually corrupting the signal.
The Microstructure Mismatch

Why does volume normalisation fail? It comes down to who is trading. Informed institutional traders scale their positions based on capacity—which is proportional to the firm's Market Capitalisation. Noise traders, on the other hand, trade based on daily liquidity—which is proportional to Trading Volume.

When you divide raw order flow by trading volume, you are mathematically multiplying the true informed signal by the inverse of turnover (1 / Turnover). Because daily turnover is incredibly volatile and stock-specific, you introduce massive heteroskedastic noise. You've essentially put your clean signal through a blender before feeding it to your neural network.
Enter the Matched Filter

In signal processing, a matched filter is a filter designed to maximise the signal-to-noise ratio by matching the known structure of the input signal. In finance, if informed traders scale by market cap, then the matched filter is simple: divide raw order flow by Market Capitalisation, not trading volume.

In a horse-race regression on 2.7 million stock-days, the market-cap-normalised flow predicted next-day returns with a massive t-statistic of 9.65. The volume-normalised flow? Barely significant at t = 2.10, and it actually reversed sign in joint regressions, proving it was just picking up spurious noise.

Even better, in his follow-up paper, 'The Limits of Complexity', Kang showed that a simple linear model using this 'Matched Filter' preprocessing achieved a Sharpe ratio of 1.30. Meanwhile, a complex ICA-Wavelet-LSTM pipeline thrown at poorly normalised data collapsed entirely, delivering a Sharpe of 0.07.
Python Implementation

def extract_signals(df):
    # df contains: 'net_flow_usd', 'market_cap_usd', 'volume_usd'
    
    # Flawed Way: Volume Normalisation (injects noise)
    df['signal_volume_norm'] = df['net_flow_usd'] / df['volume_usd']
    
    # Matched Filter Way: Market Cap Normalisation
    df['signal_matched_filter'] = df['net_flow_usd'] / df['market_cap_usd']
    
    return df
The Interview & Pub Conversation Angle

items: The 'Keep It Simple' Argument: Next time someone suggests throwing a Transformer or LSTM at a low signal-to-noise dataset, ask them: 'Have we actually matched our preprocessing to the scaling behaviour of the signal generator?' It sounds incredibly smart and is highly practical.

The 'Informed Executor' Hypothesis: The paper also notes that while domestic institutions scale by market cap, foreign institutions (who often use VWAP/TWAP algorithms) scale by trading value. Thus, the optimal matched filter depends on who you are tracking.

The Pitfall of Inverse Turnover: Remember that dividing by volume is mathematically equivalent to multiplying by the inverse of turnover. If turnover is highly volatile, you are just injecting heteroskedasticity.

content.text: Risks & Limitations

While market-cap normalisation works beautifully for capacity-constrained institutional flows, it might not be the optimal matched filter for retail flows or high-frequency market makers who are strictly bound by daily volume constraints. You must always match the filter to the specific agent's constraints.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: If you have spent any time on LinkedIn or tech Twitter lately, you have probably seen some evangelist claiming that 'AI agents' are about to replace entire corporate C-suites. Well, a group of researchers from Georgia Tech, Columbia, and The Fin AI decided to actually put that to the test. They built a simulator called EnterpriseArena to see if LLMs could cut it as a Chief Financial Officer (CFO). Spoiler alert: most of them ended up in simulated liquidation.
The paper is titled 'Can LLM Agents Be CFOs? Benchmarking Long-Horizon Resource Allocation in an Uncertain Enterprise Environment' (arXiv:2603.23638) by Yi Han, Yan Wang, Lingfei Qian, et al.
Why This One?

Most AI benchmarks are 'toy' setups. They ask an LLM to write a Python script, summarise a PDF, or answer a trivia question where the feedback is instant and the stakes are zero. This paper forces LLMs to play the long game. It simulates an 11-year (132-month) business cycle at a FinTech lending firm. The agent acts as the CFO and must manage liquidity, close the books, raise equity or debt, and navigate macroeconomic shifts. Crucially, actions are irreversible, consequences are delayed, and information is not free—the agent has to pay to see its own financial reports, forcing a trade-off between buying data and conserving cash.
The Detailed Summary & Shocking Results
The researchers ran 23 different LLMs through the simulator using various agent frameworks. The results are a glorious reality check for the AI hype machine:

items: A 15.4% Survival Rate: Across all trials, only 15.4% of the LLM agents managed to survive the full 11-year horizon without going bust. The rest triggered catastrophic liquidity crises or outright bankruptcy.

Size Does Not Matter: In a hilarious twist, model scale did not predict success. An 8B Llama-3.1 model achieved a terminal firm value of $30.6M—nearly double the $16.0M achieved by the massive 397B Qwen3.5-MoE, and higher than all seven closed-source frontier models tested.

The Human Baseline is Safe: Human experts achieved a 100% survival rate and an average terminal value of $476.7M. The absolute best-performing AI setup (GPT-5.5 using a specialized framework) only managed $34.7M—just 7% of the human expert baseline.
The Failure Cascade: LLMs struggled heavily with 'delayed consequences.' They would either freeze and fail to raise capital when conditions were good, or panic-buy expensive data and run out of cash.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: The Strategy Bottleneck: LLMs are excellent at reactive, short-term tasks, but they are fundamentally broken when it comes to long-term resource allocation under uncertainty.
The High Win-Rate Trap: Many models optimised for short-term, high-probability wins but completely ignored tail risks, leading to sudden, irreversible ruin.
Information is Costly: In the real world, you do not have perfect information. The fact that LLMs had to 'pay' to see their balance sheets completely threw off their decision-making loops.

content.text: What the Authors Say

"Unlike reactive tasks with immediate feedback, this setting requires agents to make binding commitments under partial observability, delayed consequences, hard resource budgets, and shifting dynamics... current agents remain far from robust."
What to Skim vs. What to Read

Skip the dense mathematical formulations of the environment's transition dynamics in Section 3. Instead, focus on Section 4 (Experimental Results) and the Failure Analysis section. The qualitative breakdown of why the models failed—specifically how they misjudged capital sizing and timing—is a masterclass in the limitations of probabilistic systems.
How This Connects to You & What to Say at the Pub

If you work in asset management, corporate finance, or venture capital, this paper is your shield against the 'AI is taking our jobs next week' crowd. It proves that strategic foresight, patience, and risk management are still uniquely human domains.
Next time someone at work or over a pint of Guinness starts hyping up autonomous AI corporations, you can drop this:

"Have you seen the EnterpriseArena paper? They ran 23 LLMs as simulated CFOs over an 11-year business cycle, and 84% of them went bankrupt. The funniest part is that an open-source 8B model actually beat a 397B model. It turns out scaling parameters does not give a model strategic foresight—they just over-analyse themselves into liquidation."
The Sharpe Pint Take

This paper is brilliant because it exposes the core weakness of current LLM architectures: they do not actually understand time or risk. They predict the next token based on historical patterns, which works fine when you are writing an email, but is lethal when you are managing a balance sheet through a recession. For now, your job is safe. If anything, this paper suggests that the future of finance is not AI replacing the CFO; it is humans using AI to automate the boring admin so we have more time to prevent the AI from bankrupting the company.

sources.title: Can LLM Agents Be CFOs? Benchmarking Long-Horizon Resource Allocation in an Uncertain Enterprise Environment
sources.note: This paper introduces EnterpriseArena, a benchmark evaluating LLM agents on long-horizon resource allocation, showing that 84% of models fail to survive as simulated CFOs.

content.text: The Uniqueness Trap: Why your 'special snowflake' project is doomed to overrun

We've all sat in a meeting where a project sponsor or a keen VP of Change Management slides a deck across the table and declares, with absolute conviction: 'This is a completely bespoke, ground-up transformation. There's nothing else like it in the market.' It sounds exciting. It wins budget. But according to Oxford research, it is also the kiss of death.

This is known as Uniqueness Bias (or the Uniqueness Trap). It is the cognitive tendency of planners and managers to view their projects, deals, or organisations as highly singular and 'one-of-a-kind'. A landmark paper by Bent Flyvbjerg and Alexander Budzier at Oxford's Saïd Business School analysed hundreds of major projects and found a direct, statistically significant link between how 'unique' managers believed their project was and how spectacularly it underperformed.

Why do we do it? Partly because the industry rewards it. The Project Management Institute literally defines a project as a 'temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result'. But mostly, it's an ego trip. Believing your project is unique allows you to ignore historical data, disregard past failures, and bypass what Daniel Kahneman called 'decision hygiene'. If you're unique, the 70% failure rate of M&A integrations or the notorious cost overruns of bank IT overhauls simply don't apply to you. You're special.
In the City, this manifests in three classic ways:

items: The Bespoke Software Obsession: Refusing to buy off-the-shelf portfolio management or CRM systems because 'our workflow is too unique,' leading to a five-year, multi-million-pound custom build that eventually gets scrapped.
The 'Synergistic' M&A Deal: Justifying a massive premium on an acquisition because 'this combination is entirely unique,' ignoring the graveyard of identical deals in the sector.
The Proprietary Model: Quants or portfolio managers refusing to benchmark their new strategy against historical regimes because 'the market dynamics today are completely unprecedented.'

content.text: How to use it this week:

Next time a colleague or boss pitches a project as 'completely unique,' politely pull the handbrake. Ask them: 'If we had to find three historical projects that are at least 80% similar to this, what would they be, and how did they actually turn out?' This forces the team into what Kahneman called the 'Outside View' (or Reference Class Forecasting). It strips away the romanticism of the 'bespoke' and forces people to look at the cold, hard base rates. If you can't find a single analogue, you aren't being innovative; you're just flying blind.
"You're absolutely unique, just like everyone else." — Margaret Mead (popularised by Bent Flyvbjerg)
